highlightAliases.old: Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH, normal free T4/T3; prevalence 1-6%, persistence >50% on repeat testing. Treatment is now recommended (increased AF, heart failure, CV mortality, fracture, dementia risk) (p1551).
highlightAliases.new: Subclinical hyperthyroidism = low TSH, normal free T4/T3; prevalence 1-6%, persistence >50% on repeat testing. Confirm persistence. For adults aged 65 and older with endogenous subclinical hyperthyroidism, the ATA recommends treatment when TSH stays below 0.1 mU/L, and consideration of treatment when it remains between 0.1 mU/L and the lower reference limit. Consider symptoms, cardiac disease and osteoporosis (p1551). ATA recommendations 83 and 85.

highlightAliases.old: Myxedema coma: give IV hydrocortisone before/with thyroid hormone — treating with thyroid hormone alone can precipitate adrenal crisis. Initial levothyroxine 200-400 μg, then 75-100 μg/day; avoid added T3 (cardiac risk) (p1553).
highlightAliases.new: Myxedema coma: give IV hydrocortisone before/with thyroid hormone — treating with thyroid hormone alone can precipitate adrenal crisis. Initial IV levothyroxine 200–400 μg, using the lower end for older patients or those with cardiac disease, then the chapter gives 75–100 μg/day. Rapid T3 exposure may increase cardiac risk (p1553; ATA recommendation 21a).

highlightAliases.old: Full replacement dose in older adults is lower than the young-adult 1.6 μg/kg/day; "start low, go slow" in patients ≥65 with cardiac disease, using 25-50 μg tablets (p1552).
highlightAliases.new: Full replacement dose in older adults is lower than the young-adult 1.6 μg/kg/day. With known coronary artery disease, start oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 μg/day and increase cautiously according to symptoms and TSH (p1552, ATA section 4b).

highlightAliases.old: Benign-nodule follow-up: repeat ultrasound in 12-18 months, then surveillance every 2-5 years. A nodule with two benign FNAs needs no further aspiration (p1556).
highlightAliases.new: After a benign FNA, match surveillance to ultrasound risk. High suspicion calls for repeat ultrasound and US-guided FNA within 12 months. Low or intermediate suspicion calls for ultrasound at 12–24 months. With very low suspicion, wait at least 24 months if rescanning. Two benign US-guided FNAs end routine surveillance for malignancy in that nodule (p1556, ATA recommendation 23).

highlightAliases.old: The chapter cites 25–50 micrograms as reasonable starting doses.
highlightAliases.new: The chapter gives 25–50 micrograms as examples. For stable primary hypothyroidism with known coronary artery disease, the ATA advises starting oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 micrograms daily and titrating to symptoms and TSH (ATA, section 4b).

highlightAliases.old: After a benign aspirate, repeat ultrasound initially at 12–18 months.
highlightAliases.new: After a first benign aspirate, page 1556 gives an initial ultrasound interval of 12–18 months. ATA recommendation 23 uses the ultrasound pattern. A highly suspicious nodule needs repeat ultrasound and US-guided aspiration within 12 months. For low or intermediate suspicion, repeat ultrasound at 12–24 months. For very low suspicion, any repeat scan should be at least 24 months later.

highlightAliases.old: With two benign aspirates the likelihood of two false negatives is very low.
highlightAliases.new: After two benign US-guided aspirates, cancer surveillance of that nodule can stop. A large nodule may still need review if it causes pressure symptoms (ATA, recommendation 23).

highlightAliases.old: "Start low, go slow" using the smallest tablets (25-50 μg).
highlightAliases.new: For stable primary hypothyroidism with known coronary artery disease, start oral levothyroxine at 12.5–25 μg daily and titrate gradually according to cardiac symptoms and TSH (ATA section 4b).
